round1.cite: each premise a scope proposal rests on is run in code on HEAD before the scope window opens
round1.reply:
Support-it

The design is minimal. It adds no seat, file or meeting, and the facilitator's check (C4) is a mechanical read of the proposal file in git: each premise line has a command, a HEAD hash and an output line, or the word "unrun". The "unrun" label is a sound release valve. It also has the 229-scope-2 evidence behind it.

The weak point is C1. Whether a line "states how existing code or tests behave" is a judgment call, so a proposer can leave a premise out without the check noticing. Counter-metric 3 covers this only after the fact. I'd tighten it by requiring every Assumes or Probe line to carry a command or "unrun", with no exemption for lines the proposer calls non-premises.

round1.cite: each premise a scope proposal rests on is run in code on HEAD
round1.reply:
Support-it

The rule fits the card 229 failure. Running red 2 with scrub-then-trim would have shown both disproved premises before the window opened. The trial is a two-way door, and counter-metric 3 guards against premise lines being dropped.

My reservations are about what the check can catch:
- C4 checks the form of a premise line, not whether the quoted output is true. A made-up output line would pass the facilitator's look, and only the auditor's re-check from git would catch it.
- The "unrun" label is open to overuse. Counter-metric 3 only catches premise lines disappearing, not premises being labelled unrun.
- The metric starts from a baseline of one event.

None of these should block a trial.

round1.reply:
Yes

As the developer, I can comply with this without gaming it. A probe per premise is one command, such as a `python -c` line or the existing red run with my change applied locally and discarded. That is cheap next to a second scope window. C1 limits premises to lines about how existing code or tests behave, so I'm not asked to probe opinions. C3's "unrun" label plus a stated fallback is an honest release valve, so I don't have to fake output. Counter-metric 3 guards against fewer premise lines being passed off as fewer risks. The one wrinkle: "HEAD hash" may drift if HEAD moves before the window, but that is minor.

round1.cite: each premise a scope proposal rests on is run in code on HEAD
round1.reply:
Support-it

The practice is mostly checkable from git alone. The proposal file has to carry a command, a HEAD hash and an output line, or "unrun", for each premise. A missing one sends it back before any vote, and the auditor re-checks from git.

There are two loopholes:
- **Unrun label:** "unrun" is a free pass. Counter-metric 3 only catches premises that go unstated, not ones that are never run.
- **Quoted output:** git can't show that the output was really produced. The auditor can re-run the command at the quoted HEAD, so the sign-off should say to do that for at least one premise per card.

Neither blocks a reversible, three-card trial.

rerun.cite: each premise a scope proposal rests on is run in code on HEAD
rerun.reply:
Support-it

The practice can mostly be checked from git. The proposal file must carry a command, a HEAD hash and an output line per premise, so the auditor can check out that hash and re-run the command.

There is one loophole. "Unrun" is free, because C3 sets no cap and no reason requirement. A team could label every premise "unrun" and pass C4 while still breaking the practice. Counter-metric 3 only catches premises that go unstated. It doesn't catch ones marked "unrun".

Two fixes would close it. The sign-off should count unrun premises per proposal, and the auditor should flag any premise marked "unrun" that could have been run in seconds. Also, "caused by a premise" is a judgment call, so the sign-off should name the disproving test or commit.
